proQuiz.q: When asked to assess something in Mathematics, you should:
opts: List all relevant facts
Define key terms only
Weigh importance using specific evidence then reach a justified conclusion
Describe the process
proQuiz.exp: Assess = weigh and judge. Consider multiple factors, provide evidence, decide which factor is most significant and explain why. Every point must be evaluated, not just described.

proQuiz.q: Which distinguishes a Grade 9 from a Grade 7 response in Mathematics?
opts: Length
Quantity of facts
Consistent perceptive evaluative analysis — non-obvious insights, significance evaluation, nuanced conclusions
Handwriting quality
proQuiz.exp: AQA Grade 9: perceptive, convincing, nuanced. Grade 7: detailed, clear, well-developed. Grade 9 requires going beyond description to genuine insight and evaluation throughout the response.

proQuiz.q: For 9-mark questions in Mathematics, the most effective structure is:
opts: Three points as a list
Introduction + 3 developed analytical points with evidence + counterargument + conclusion with overall judgement
Just one very long point
Only counterarguments
proQuiz.exp: 9-mark structure: three analytical points (each with claim + evidence + analysis) + counterargument + conclusion that directly answers the question with a justified verdict.

proQuiz.q: How should you use specific data in Mathematics exam answers?
opts: Avoid numbers as they might be wrong
Include specific figures, dates, and named examples to support each claim — vague answers score much lower
Only in science subjects
At the end of answers only
proQuiz.exp: Specific evidence: named examples, precise statistics, exact dates score more than vague claims. The specificity demonstrates genuine knowledge rather than generic understanding.

proQuiz.q: Interleaving Vectors with other topics during revision is beneficial because:
opts: It is easier
It creates retrieval challenges that build stronger, more flexible memory traces
It covers topics superficially
It reduces study time significantly
proQuiz.exp: Interleaving (mixing topics in one session) is more effortful but produces better retention than blocked study. The brain is forced to identify which knowledge applies — building flexible, transferable understanding.

proQuiz.q: A model answer for Vectors should be used to:
opts: Memorise word for word
Analyse why it scores highly — structure, evidence, connectives, terminology — then practise the same SKILLS independently
Submit as your own work
Ignore since it was written by someone else
proQuiz.exp: Model answers reveal examiner expectations. Analyse: what structure did they use? Which evidence? What connectives? How is the conclusion phrased? Understand WHY it scores, then develop those skills yourself.

proQuiz.q: When revising Vectors, spaced retrieval practice means:
opts: Studying for long sessions without breaks
Testing yourself at increasing time intervals — day 1, day 3, day 7, day 14 — each session reinforcing memory traces
Reading notes repeatedly
Studying only the night before
proQuiz.exp: Spaced retrieval (Ebbinghaus): memory strength decays but is rebuilt stronger each time you retrieve it. Increasing the gaps between retrieval sessions maximises long-term retention with less total study time.

proQuiz.q: What makes evidence in Mathematics answers most persuasive?
opts: Using long quotations or data tables
Selecting the most directly relevant specific evidence, embedding it within your argument, and explaining precisely how it supports your claim
Including as much evidence as possible
Evidence from personal experience
proQuiz.exp: Evidence quality > quantity. One precisely relevant, well-interpreted piece of evidence scores higher than three loosely relevant ones. Always explain the connection: "This evidence suggests that... because..."

proQuiz.q: In extended writing about Vectors, which connectives best demonstrate analytical thinking?
opts: And, but, also
Therefore, consequently, this demonstrates that, nevertheless, on balance, this suggests — creating logical chains between evidence and argument
However is the only useful connective
Connectives are not important
proQuiz.exp: Analytical connectives create explicit logical chains: evidence + therefore + interpretation + however + counterargument + on balance + conclusion. They show the examiner HOW your evidence supports your argument.

proQuiz.q: Why is it important to address counterarguments in extended answers?
opts: It is not — just argue one side strongly
Acknowledging and refuting counterarguments shows sophisticated understanding and strengthens your position by demonstrating you have considered the full picture
Present only counterarguments
The counterargument should be your conclusion
proQuiz.exp: Counterarguments demonstrate: understanding of complexity, that your position has survived scrutiny, and analytical sophistication. Some argue X, however this is outweighed by Y because Z — this structure scores Level 4.

proQuiz.q: What is the difference between an assertion and an argument in Mathematics?
opts: They are identical
An assertion states a claim without support. An argument provides claim + evidence + reasoning linking the two. Assertions score Level 1-2; arguments score Level 3-4.
Arguments are longer than assertions
Assertions use better vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Assertion: X is important. Argument: X is the most significant factor because Y (evidence), which demonstrates Z, making it more influential than alternative A due to B. The mechanism and comparative judgement elevate assertion to argument.

proQuiz.q: Past exam papers for Vectors are best used by:
opts: Reading them without attempting
Attempting under timed conditions, then self-marking rigorously, identifying your current level, studying Level 4 exemplars, and practising specific identified weaknesses
Only reading the mark scheme
Skipping difficult questions
proQuiz.exp: Past paper practice cycle: (1) attempt under exam conditions; (2) mark against official mark scheme; (3) identify level achieved; (4) study Level 4 responses to see what Level 4 requires; (5) practise the specific skills you lack.

proQuiz.q: How does the testing effect help with Vectors?
opts: Testing is discouraging and should be avoided
Being tested on material — even before feeling ready — improves long-term retention more than equivalent re-study time. Retrieval strengthens memory traces.
Testing only measures not improves learning
Testing works only for factual recall
proQuiz.exp: Testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006): retrieval practice is one of the most effective learning strategies. The effort of trying to recall information strengthens the memory trace even more than re-reading. Struggle during recall is a sign of productive learning.

proQuiz.q: What does "perceptive" mean in AQA mark scheme language for Mathematics?
opts: Simply correct and detailed
Showing insight beyond the obvious — making non-trivial connections, noticing subtle implications, offering original interpretations that demonstrate deep understanding
Writing at length
Using complex vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Perceptive is AQA's highest-level analytical descriptor. It implies going beyond the explicitly stated to infer, interpret, and connect ideas in original ways. Perceptive students notice what is NOT said as much as what IS said.

proQuiz.q: You understand Vectors deeply if you can:
opts: Recite your notes from memory
Apply the concepts to unfamiliar exam questions, explain them in your own words, identify connections to other topics, and evaluate conflicting evidence confidently
Re-read your notes without hesitation
Score 100% on a familiar quiz
proQuiz.exp: True mastery = transfer. If you can only answer questions you've seen before, you have surface learning. Deep learning enables flexible application to ANY question on the topic, regardless of phrasing or context.

proQuiz.q: For Vectors, which study approach creates the deepest understanding?
opts: Re-reading textbook chapters
Trying to TEACH the concept to someone else (real or imaginary) — the effort of explanation forces you to identify gaps and restructure knowledge
Making colourful notes
Listening to recorded lessons
proQuiz.exp: The protege effect: teaching consolidates understanding. When you explain a concept, you identify precisely where your understanding breaks down — this guides targeted revision. The Feynman technique: if you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it deeply.

proQuiz.q: When writing a conclusion for an extended Mathematics answer:
opts: Simply repeat your first point
Directly answer the question stating which argument is most significant and why
Write a new argument not in the body
Write: in conclusion there are many factors
proQuiz.exp: Effective conclusions: directly answer the question using on balance or therefore. State your overall judgement with reasoning. Base it on body evidence only. Never introduce new points in a conclusion.

name: Functions & Further Algebra

points: A function maps each input to exactly one output. Notation: f(x) = 3x - 2 means "the function f of x equals 3x - 2". To evaluate: substitute the value. f(5) = 3(5) - 2 = 13.
Composite functions fg(x): apply g first, then f. fg(x) = f(g(x)). Example: if f(x) = 2x+1 and g(x) = x², then fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x²+1. Note: fg(x) ≠ gf(x) in general.
Inverse function f⁻¹(x): reverses the function. To find: let y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange for y. Example: f(x) = 3x-2. Let y=3x-2. Swap: x=3y-2. Rearrange: y=(x+2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x+2)/3.
Iteration: a numerical method to find approximate roots of equations. Given an iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ), start with an initial estimate x₀ and repeatedly apply the formula.
The iteration converges to a root of the equation x = f(x) (equivalently f(x) - x = 0). A "staircase" or "cobweb" diagram shows this visually.

Algebraic fractions: apply normal fraction rules. To add/subtract: find a common denominator. To multiply: multiply numerators and denominators. To divide: flip the second fraction (multiply by its reciprocal). Always simplify by factorising first.
Equations with algebraic fractions: multiply through by the LCM of denominators to clear fractions, then solve the resulting polynomial equation.

flashcards.q: f(x) = 5x + 3, g(x) = x². Find fg(4).
flashcards.a: fg(4) = f(g(4)). Step 1: g(4) = 4² = 16. Step 2: f(16) = 5(16)+3 = 83. So fg(4) = 83. Remember: composite functions work from RIGHT to LEFT — evaluate the rightmost function first. fg(x) ≠ gf(x): gf(4) = g(f(4)) = g(23) = 529.

flashcards.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 4x - 7.
flashcards.a: Step 1: write y = 4x - 7. Step 2: swap x and y: x = 4y - 7. Step 3: rearrange for y: 4y = x + 7, y = (x+7)/4. So f⁻¹(x) = (x+7)/4. Check: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 4×(x+7)/4 - 7 = x+7-7 = x ✓

flashcards.q: Simplify the algebraic fraction (x²-4)/(x²+x-6).
flashcards.a: Factorise numerator: x²-4 = (x+2)(x-2). Factorise denominator: x²+x-6 = (x+3)(x-2). Cancel common factor (x-2): result = (x+2)/(x+3). This is valid for x ≠ 2. Always factorise completely before attempting to cancel.

flashcards.q: Using the iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = √(5+xₙ), starting with x₀=2, find x₂.
flashcards.a: x₁ = √(5+2) = √7 ≈ 2.6458. x₂ = √(5+2.6458) = √7.6458 ≈ 2.7651. This converges to the positive root of x = √(5+x), i.e. x² = 5+x, i.e. x²-x-5=0. The root ≈ 2.7913.
Multiply through by (x+1)(x-2): 3(x-2)+2(x+1) = (x+1)(x-2). Left: 3x-6+2x+2 = 5x-4. Right: x²-x-2. Equation: x²-x-2=5x-4 → x²-6x+2=0. Quadratic formula: x=(6±√(36-8))/2=(6±√28)/2=3±√7.

flashcards.q: What are the four types of transformations?
flashcards.a: Translation (vector), Rotation (centre + angle + direction), Reflection (mirror line), Enlargement (centre + scale factor)

flashcards.q: How do you describe a rotation fully?
flashcards.a: Centre of rotation, angle, direction (clockwise/anticlockwise)

flashcards.q: How do you describe a translation?
flashcards.a: Using a column vector: (x/y) where x = right/left movement, y = up/down movement

flashcards.q: What is a scale factor of -2 enlargement?
flashcards.a: Enlarges by factor 2 AND reflects through the centre of enlargement (negative scale factor = through the centre)

flashcards.q: How do you find the centre of rotation?
flashcards.a: Draw perpendicular bisectors of two pairs of corresponding points — they intersect at the centre

flashcards.q: What are invariant points?
flashcards.a: Points that do not move under a transformation — every point on a mirror line is invariant under reflection

flashcards.q: How do you find the inverse transformation?
flashcards.a: Undo the original: inverse of translation (a/b) is (-a/-b). Inverse rotation: same centre, opposite direction

flashcards.q: What does a column vector (3/-2) describe?
flashcards.a: Move 3 units right and 2 units down

flashcards.q: What is a combined transformation?
flashcards.a: Applying two or more transformations in sequence — the order matters

flashcards.q: What is a matrix used for in transformations?
flashcards.a: A 2×2 matrix can represent rotations, reflections and enlargements as linear transformations

tips.t: "fg" means "f of g" — apply g FIRST then f. Many students get this backwards. Read right to left: fg(x) = f(g(x)). Mnemonic: the function closest to x acts first. fg ≠ gf in general — always check which order is asked.
Steps for f⁻¹: (1) Write y=f(x). (2) Swap x and y. (3) Rearrange for y. (4) Write as f⁻¹(x)=... Check your answer by verifying f(f⁻¹(x))=x.

quiz.q: f(x) = 2x + 1. Find f⁻¹(x).
quiz.exp: Let y=2x+1. Swap: x=2y+1. Rearrange: 2y=x-1, y=(x-1)/2. So f⁻¹(x)=(x-1)/2. Check: f(f⁻¹(x))=2×(x-1)/2+1=x-1+1=x ✓

quiz.q: f(x) = x² + 1 and g(x) = 3x. Find gf(2).
quiz.exp: gf(2) = g(f(2)). f(2) = 4+1=5. g(5)=3×5=15. So gf(2)=15. Note: gf means apply f first, then g. If the question asked fg(2): g(2)=6, f(6)=37.

quiz.q: Simplify (2x²+5x+3)/(x²-1).
quiz.exp: Factorise numerator: 2x²+5x+3=(2x+3)(x+1). Factorise denominator: x²-1=(x+1)(x-1). Cancel (x+1): result=(2x+3)/(x-1). Valid for x≠-1 and x≠1.

quiz.q: The iterative formula xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ²+3)/4 is used starting with x₀=2. Find x₁.
quiz.exp: x₁=(x₀²+3)/4=(4+3)/4=7/4=1.75. Continue: x₂=(1.75²+3)/4=(3.0625+3)/4=1.516. This converges to a root of x=(x²+3)/4, i.e. 4x=x²+3, i.e. x²-4x+3=0=(x-1)(x-3). Roots are x=1 and x=3.

quiz.q: If f(x) = (x+3)/2 and g(x) = 4x-1, find fg(x).
quiz.exp: fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(4x-1) = ((4x-1)+3)/2 = (4x+2)/2 = 2x+1. Apply g first (giving 4x-1) then substitute that into f.

quiz.q: What is the domain restriction for f(x) = 1/(x-3)?
quiz.exp: f(x) = 1/(x-3) is undefined when the denominator = 0, i.e. when x-3=0, so x=3. Therefore the domain is all real numbers except x=3 (written x ∈ ℝ, x ≠ 3). AQA: the domain excludes values that make a denominator zero or a square root negative.

quiz.q: Find ff(x) if f(x) = 3x - 2.
quiz.exp: ff(x) = f(f(x)) = f(3x-2) = 3(3x-2)-2 = 9x-6-2 = 9x-8. To find ff(x), substitute f(x) as the input into f. This is the same as finding the composite function where f is composed with itself.

quiz.q: Simplify 3/(x+2) + 2/(x-1).
quiz.exp: Common denominator: (x+2)(x-1). Numerator: 3(x-1)+2(x+2)=3x-3+2x+4=5x+1. Answer: (5x+1)/((x+2)(x-1)). Always find the common denominator first, multiply each numerator accordingly, then add.

quiz.q: The equation x³-5x+1=0 has a root near x=2. Using the rearrangement xₙ₊₁=∛(5xₙ-1), find x₁ if x₀=2.
quiz.exp: x₁=∛(5×2-1)=∛(9)≈2.080... wait, ∛9=2.0801. So x₁≈2.080. Actually let me recalculate: 5×2-1=9, ∛9≈2.0801. So the answer is approximately 2.080, which corresponds to option C. But let me check option A: 2.154 would mean ∛9.996≈2.154 — no. Answer: C (2.080). [AQA: always show the substitution clearly.]

quiz.q: Solve: x/(x+1) + 1/(x-2) = 1. (Choose the correct equation after multiplying through.)
quiz.exp: Multiply every term by (x+1)(x-2): x(x-2)+1(x+1)=(x+1)(x-2). Expand: x²-2x+x+1=x²-x-2. Simplify: x²-x+1=x²-x-2. This gives 1=-2, a contradiction — so this equation has NO solution.

quiz.q: If f(x)=2x+5, what is f(f⁻¹(7))?
quiz.exp: f(f⁻¹(x))=x for any function and its inverse. This is the definition of an inverse function — applying f then f⁻¹ (or f⁻¹ then f) always returns the original input. So f(f⁻¹(7))=7 directly, without needing to find f⁻¹.

quiz.q: A translation by vector (3, -2) moves every point:
opts: Replacing variables with numbers to evaluate an expression
An plus b giving any term when n is the position number

quiz.exp: Translation vector: top number = horizontal movement (positive = right, negative = left). Bottom number = vertical movement (positive = up, negative = down). Translating point (1, 4) by (3, -2): new point = (1+3, 4-2) = (4, 2). Translation: does not change the size, shape or orientation of the object — just its position.

proQuiz.q: Interleaving Functions & Further Algebra with other topics during revision is beneficial because:
opts: It is easier
It creates retrieval challenges that build stronger, more flexible memory traces
It covers topics superficially
It reduces study time significantly
proQuiz.exp: Interleaving (mixing topics in one session) is more effortful but produces better retention than blocked study. The brain is forced to identify which knowledge applies — building flexible, transferable understanding.

proQuiz.q: A model answer for Functions & Further Algebra should be used to:
opts: Memorise word for word
Analyse why it scores highly — structure, evidence, connectives, terminology — then practise the same SKILLS independently
Submit as your own work
Ignore since it was written by someone else
proQuiz.exp: Model answers reveal examiner expectations. Analyse: what structure did they use? Which evidence? What connectives? How is the conclusion phrased? Understand WHY it scores, then develop those skills yourself.

proQuiz.q: When revising Functions & Further Algebra, spaced retrieval practice means:
opts: Studying for long sessions without breaks
Testing yourself at increasing time intervals — day 1, day 3, day 7, day 14 — each session reinforcing memory traces
Reading notes repeatedly
Studying only the night before
proQuiz.exp: Spaced retrieval (Ebbinghaus): memory strength decays but is rebuilt stronger each time you retrieve it. Increasing the gaps between retrieval sessions maximises long-term retention with less total study time.

proQuiz.q: What makes evidence in Mathematics answers most persuasive?
opts: Using long quotations or data tables
Selecting the most directly relevant specific evidence, embedding it within your argument, and explaining precisely how it supports your claim
Including as much evidence as possible
Evidence from personal experience
proQuiz.exp: Evidence quality > quantity. One precisely relevant, well-interpreted piece of evidence scores higher than three loosely relevant ones. Always explain the connection: "This evidence suggests that... because..."

proQuiz.q: In extended writing about Functions & Further Algebra, which connectives best demonstrate analytical thinking?
opts: And, but, also
Therefore, consequently, this demonstrates that, nevertheless, on balance, this suggests — creating logical chains between evidence and argument
However is the only useful connective
Connectives are not important
proQuiz.exp: Analytical connectives create explicit logical chains: evidence + therefore + interpretation + however + counterargument + on balance + conclusion. They show the examiner HOW your evidence supports your argument.

proQuiz.q: Why is it important to address counterarguments in extended answers?
opts: It is not — just argue one side strongly
Acknowledging and refuting counterarguments shows sophisticated understanding and strengthens your position by demonstrating you have considered the full picture
Present only counterarguments
The counterargument should be your conclusion
proQuiz.exp: Counterarguments demonstrate: understanding of complexity, that your position has survived scrutiny, and analytical sophistication. Some argue X, however this is outweighed by Y because Z — this structure scores Level 4.

proQuiz.q: What is the difference between an assertion and an argument in Mathematics?
opts: They are identical
An assertion states a claim without support. An argument provides claim + evidence + reasoning linking the two. Assertions score Level 1-2; arguments score Level 3-4.
Arguments are longer than assertions
Assertions use better vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Assertion: X is important. Argument: X is the most significant factor because Y (evidence), which demonstrates Z, making it more influential than alternative A due to B. The mechanism and comparative judgement elevate assertion to argument.

proQuiz.q: Past exam papers for Functions & Further Algebra are best used by:
opts: Reading them without attempting
Attempting under timed conditions, then self-marking rigorously, identifying your current level, studying Level 4 exemplars, and practising specific identified weaknesses
Only reading the mark scheme
Skipping difficult questions
proQuiz.exp: Past paper practice cycle: (1) attempt under exam conditions; (2) mark against official mark scheme; (3) identify level achieved; (4) study Level 4 responses to see what Level 4 requires; (5) practise the specific skills you lack.

proQuiz.q: How does the testing effect help with Functions & Further Algebra?
opts: Testing is discouraging and should be avoided
Being tested on material — even before feeling ready — improves long-term retention more than equivalent re-study time. Retrieval strengthens memory traces.
Testing only measures not improves learning
Testing works only for factual recall
proQuiz.exp: Testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006): retrieval practice is one of the most effective learning strategies. The effort of trying to recall information strengthens the memory trace even more than re-reading. Struggle during recall is a sign of productive learning.

proQuiz.q: What does "perceptive" mean in AQA mark scheme language for Mathematics?
opts: Simply correct and detailed
Showing insight beyond the obvious — making non-trivial connections, noticing subtle implications, offering original interpretations that demonstrate deep understanding
Writing at length
Using complex vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Perceptive is AQA's highest-level analytical descriptor. It implies going beyond the explicitly stated to infer, interpret, and connect ideas in original ways. Perceptive students notice what is NOT said as much as what IS said.

proQuiz.q: You understand Functions & Further Algebra deeply if you can:
opts: Recite your notes from memory
Apply the concepts to unfamiliar exam questions, explain them in your own words, identify connections to other topics, and evaluate conflicting evidence confidently
Re-read your notes without hesitation
Score 100% on a familiar quiz
proQuiz.exp: True mastery = transfer. If you can only answer questions you've seen before, you have surface learning. Deep learning enables flexible application to ANY question on the topic, regardless of phrasing or context.

proQuiz.q: For Functions & Further Algebra, which study approach creates the deepest understanding?
opts: Re-reading textbook chapters
Trying to TEACH the concept to someone else (real or imaginary) — the effort of explanation forces you to identify gaps and restructure knowledge
Making colourful notes
Listening to recorded lessons
proQuiz.exp: The protege effect: teaching consolidates understanding. When you explain a concept, you identify precisely where your understanding breaks down — this guides targeted revision. The Feynman technique: if you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it deeply.

proQuiz.q: When writing a conclusion for an extended Mathematics answer:
opts: Simply repeat your first point
Directly answer the question stating which argument is most significant and why
Write a new argument not in the body
Write: in conclusion there are many factors
proQuiz.exp: Effective conclusions: directly answer the question using on balance or therefore. State your overall judgement with reasoning. Base it on body evidence only. Never introduce new points in a conclusion.

proTip: Pro Tip for Mathematics - Functions & Further Algebra: Always use specific evidence, precise terminology, and evaluate every claim. Structure: point + evidence + analysis + evaluation. Target your weakest sub-topics using your quiz results.

name: Constructions, Loci & Bearings

points: All constructions require a compass and ruler. Never erase construction arcs — they show your method and earn marks.

Perpendicular bisector of AB: open compass to more than half AB. Draw arcs above and below from A. Repeat from B with same radius. Join the two intersection points. This line is the perpendicular bisector.
Angle bisector: open compass from vertex to cut both arms. From each cut point, draw equal arcs that intersect. Join the intersection to the vertex.
Perpendicular from a point to a line: from the point, draw an arc cutting the line at two points. From each, draw arcs that intersect below the line. Join to original point.

A locus is the set of all points satisfying a given rule. Common loci: (1) Points equidistant from a fixed point → circle. (2) Points equidistant from two fixed points → perpendicular bisector. (3) Points equidistant from two lines → angle bisector. (4) Points at a fixed distance from a line → parallel lines with semicircular ends.
Regions: shade the correct region for inequalities involving loci. "Within 3cm of A" = inside a circle radius 3cm. "Nearer to A than B" = the half of the perpendicular bisector closer to A.

Bearings: always measured clockwise from north. Always written as three figures (045°, not 45°). Back bearing: if bearing from A to B is θ, then bearing from B to A is θ + 180° (if θ < 180°) or θ - 180° (if θ ≥ 180°).

flashcards.q: What is the locus of all points equidistant from two fixed points A and B?
flashcards.a: The perpendicular bisector of the line segment AB. Every point on this line is exactly the same distance from A as from B. The perpendicular bisector bisects AB at right angles. AQA: this is the most frequently tested locus. Always draw it with full construction arcs to gain method marks.

flashcards.q: What is the locus of points equidistant from two straight lines?
flashcards.a: The angle bisector(s) of the two lines. There are two angle bisectors (perpendicular to each other) for two intersecting lines. For a corner or angle, the angle bisector is the locus of points equidistant from both sides.

flashcards.q: State the three rules for bearings.
flashcards.a: (1) Always measured clockwise from north. (2) Always written as 3 digits (so 5° is written 005°, 45° is 045°). (3) Back bearing = forward bearing ± 180°. To convert: if bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If bearing is 180° or more, subtract 180°. Example: bearing 070° → back bearing is 250°.

flashcards.q: How do you construct an angle bisector?
flashcards.a: Step 1: Place compass at the vertex, draw an arc cutting both arms of the angle. Step 2: From each point where the arc crosses the arms, draw equal arcs that cross each other. Step 3: Draw a straight line from the vertex through the intersection of the arcs. Do not erase construction marks — they earn marks in AQA.

flashcards.q: What region represents points within 4 cm of point A AND closer to B than to C?
flashcards.a: The intersection of: (1) The interior of a circle radius 4 cm centred at A, AND (2) The half-plane containing B on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Draw both constructions, then shade the overlapping region. AQA: for compound loci regions, always draw each locus separately first, then identify the intersection.

flashcards.q: What is standard form?
flashcards.a: A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10. Used for very large or very small numbers

flashcards.q: How do you multiply numbers in standard form?
flashcards.a: Multiply the A values, add the powers: (3×10⁴) × (2×10³) = 6×10⁷

flashcards.q: How do you add numbers in standard form?
flashcards.a: Convert to the same power first: 3×10⁴ + 2×10³ = 3×10⁴ + 0.2×10⁴ = 3.2×10⁴

flashcards.q: What is a surd?
flashcards.a: A square root that cannot be simplified to a whole number. E.g. √2, √3, √5 (not √4 = 2)

flashcards.q: How do you simplify √72?
flashcards.a: √72 = √(36×2) = 6√2 (find largest perfect square factor)

flashcards.q: How do you rationalise the denominator of 1/√3?
flashcards.a: Multiply top and bottom by √3: (1×√3)/(√3×√3) = √3/3

flashcards.q: What does it mean to estimate?
flashcards.a: Round each value to 1 significant figure, then calculate. Used to check if an answer is reasonable

flashcards.q: What is a recurring decimal?
flashcards.a: A decimal where digits repeat infinitely, e.g. 0.333... = 1/3. Convert by multiplying by 10ⁿ

flashcards.q: How do you convert a recurring decimal to a fraction?
What are bounds/limits of accuracy?
flashcards.a: The upper and lower values a rounded number could have been: 3.7 rounded to 1 d.p. → lower 3.65, upper 3.75

tips.t: AQA instructions say: "leave your construction arcs visible." If you erase them, you lose method marks even if your final line is correct. Use pencil (not pen) so you can correct mistakes without losing the arcs. Accuracy requirement: within 2mm and 2°.

For region questions: draw the boundary locus first (circle, perpendicular bisector, angle bisector, parallel lines), then shade the CORRECT side. "Within" means inside a circle (include the boundary if ≤). "Closer to A than B" means on A's side of the perpendicular bisector of AB.

quiz.q: What construction gives you all points equidistant from a given point A?
opts: Perpendicular bisector
Angle bisector
Circle centred at A
Parallel line
quiz.exp: The locus of all points at a fixed distance r from point A is a CIRCLE with centre A and radius r. All points on the circle are exactly r from A. "Within distance r from A" is the interior of the circle.

quiz.q: A ship travels on bearing 130°. What is the back bearing (the direction back to the start)?
quiz.exp: Back bearing = 130° + 180° = 310°. Rule: if forward bearing < 180°, add 180° for the back bearing. If forward bearing ≥ 180°, subtract 180°. Check: 310° - 180° = 130° ✓

quiz.q: A point P is described as "closer to line AB than to line CD, where AB and CD are parallel." What is its locus?
opts: The perpendicular bisector of AB
The region between AB and the midpoint line
theta over 360 times pi r squared where theta is the angle in degrees
The angle bisector of AB and CD
quiz.exp: For parallel lines AB and CD, the locus of points equidistant from both is a line parallel to both, halfway between them. Points closer to AB than to CD lie in the half of this region on AB's side.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT needed in a full construction of a perpendicular bisector?
opts: Compass
Ruler
Protractor
Pencil
quiz.exp: A perpendicular bisector is constructed using only a compass (for arcs) and ruler (for straight lines). A protractor is NOT used — the right angle is guaranteed by the intersection of the arcs. Erasing construction arcs will lose you marks in AQA.

quiz.q: A bearing of 045° represents which direction?
opts: North-East
South-East
North-West
South-West
quiz.exp: Bearing 045° = 45° clockwise from North = NE (North-East). Key bearings: 000°=N, 090°=E, 180°=S, 270°=W, 045°=NE, 135°=SE, 225°=SW, 315°=NW.

quiz.q: What is the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines?
opts: A circle
The perpendicular bisector
The angle bisectors of the two lines
A parallel line
quiz.exp: For two intersecting lines, the locus of equidistant points is the PAIR OF ANGLE BISECTORS. There are two bisectors, perpendicular to each other. Each bisector gives the set of points equidistant from both lines. AQA: draw both bisectors in the region.

quiz.q: A lighthouse is 5 km north and 12 km east of a harbour. What is the bearing of the lighthouse from the harbour?
quiz.exp: The angle from north: tan θ = 12/5 (east/north). θ = tan⁻¹(2.4) ≈ 67.4°. Since the lighthouse is north and east, the bearing is measured clockwise from north: bearing = 067.4° (written as 067° to nearest degree). Draw the right triangle: 5 north, 12 east.

quiz.q: Construct a region: "within 3 cm of AB AND within 2 cm of point C." Which describes the boundary?
opts: Two parallel lines and a circle
A circle only
Two parallel lines only
A rectangle
quiz.exp: "Within 3 cm of line AB" → two parallel lines (each 3 cm from AB) with semicircular ends (locus of points 3 cm from AB extended). "Within 2 cm of point C" → circle radius 2 cm centred at C. The combined region is the intersection of both, bounded by parts of the parallel lines/semicircles and the circle.

quiz.q: A plane flies from A on bearing 240°. What is the bearing of A from the plane's current position?
quiz.exp: Back bearing = 240° - 180° = 060°. Since 240° ≥ 180°, subtract 180°. The plane is looking back towards A, which is 060° (North-East direction) from the plane. Check: 060° + 180° = 240° ✓

quiz.q: Point P must be: (i) equidistant from A and B, and (ii) closer to line L than to line M. Which constructions are needed?
opts: Circle centred at A and angle bisector
Sum of all values divided by the number of values
Perpendicular bisector of AB only
Perpendicular bisector of AB and angle bisector of L and M
quiz.exp: Condition (i) equidistant from A and B → perpendicular bisector of AB. Condition (ii) closer to L than M → the angle bisector of L and M divides the plane into two regions; shade the region on the L-side. The required locus is the segment of the perpendicular bisector in the correct region.

quiz.q: What must be true for a complete bearing answer?
opts: Measured clockwise from north, written as 3 figures
A rule mapping each input x to exactly one output f(x)
Measured anticlockwise from east
Measured from the nearest compass point
quiz.exp: Bearings: ALWAYS (1) measured CLOCKWISE from NORTH and (2) written as THREE figures (digits). So 5° is written 005°, not 5°. AQA award marks specifically for the correct convention — forgetting the three-figure rule or measuring from the wrong starting point loses marks.

quiz.q: A map shows that the angle from north to a target is 35° anticlockwise. What is the bearing?
quiz.exp: Bearings are always measured CLOCKWISE from north. 35° anticlockwise from north = 360° - 35° = 325°. Written as three figures: 325°. Always convert anticlockwise angles by subtracting from 360°.

quiz.q: Standard form is useful for very large or small numbers because:
opts: In a right-angled triangle a squared plus b squared equals c squared
1cm on the map represents 50000cm which equals 500m in reality
Showing all possible outcomes with probabilities on branches
It allows numbers like 300,000,000 to be written as 3 × 10⁸ — making calculations much simpler
quiz.exp: Standard form: A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10. Large numbers: 3 × 10⁸ = 300,000,000 (speed of light in m/s). Small numbers: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ (charge on electron in coulombs). Multiplying: multiply A values and add powers. Dividing: divide A values and subtract powers. Adding/subtracting: must convert to same power first.

facts: Pi (π) has been calculated to over 100 trillion decimal places — it is irrational, meaning the digits never repeat or terminate.
The equals sign (=) was invented by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557 — he chose two parallel lines because 'no two things can be more equal'.
Every even integer greater than 2 appears to be expressible as the sum of two primes (Goldbach's Conjecture, 1742) — but this has never been proved.

definitions.def: Expressing a number as a product of its prime factors — the unique building blocks of every positive integer.
A number that cannot be expressed as a fraction p/q where p and q are integers — e.g. π, √2, e.

proQuiz.q: Which command word in Mathematics requires the most complex response?
opts: State
Describe
Evaluate — requires weighing evidence and reaching a justified conclusion
List
proQuiz.exp: Evaluate is always the highest-order command word. It requires you to weigh evidence, consider perspectives, and make a justified judgement — not just describe or explain.

proQuiz.q: For a 6-mark extended answer on Constructions, Loci & Bearings, which is essential?
opts: As many facts as possible
Specific terminology + clear argument + evidence + evaluation
Only diagrams
One-word answers
proQuiz.exp: 6-mark answers require quality reasoning using precise terminology, with specific evidence linked to a clear evaluative argument. Quantity without quality scores Level 1.

proQuiz.q: A student scores 45% on a Constructions, Loci & Bearings quiz. The best next step is:
opts: Retake immediately
Move on
Review each wrong answer, identify the specific gap, revisit notes, then retest after 24 hours
Give up on this topic
proQuiz.exp: Targeted review: identify WHAT you misunderstand, not just THAT you got it wrong. Return to notes for those specific sub-topics. Retest after a gap for spaced repetition effect.

proQuiz.q: When asked to assess something in Mathematics, you should:
opts: List all relevant facts
Define key terms only
Weigh importance using specific evidence then reach a justified conclusion
Describe the process
proQuiz.exp: Assess = weigh and judge. Consider multiple factors, provide evidence, decide which factor is most significant and explain why. Every point must be evaluated, not just described.

proQuiz.q: Which distinguishes a Grade 9 from a Grade 7 response in Mathematics?
opts: Length
Quantity of facts
Consistent perceptive evaluative analysis — non-obvious insights, significance evaluation, nuanced conclusions
Handwriting quality
proQuiz.exp: AQA Grade 9: perceptive, convincing, nuanced. Grade 7: detailed, clear, well-developed. Grade 9 requires going beyond description to genuine insight and evaluation throughout the response.

proQuiz.q: For 9-mark questions in Mathematics, the most effective structure is:

Introduction + 3 developed analytical points with evidence + counterargument + conclusion with overall judgement
Just one very long point
Only counterarguments

Write a new argument not in the body

name: Financial Mathematics

points: Simple interest: I = PRT/100. Interest is calculated only on the original principal — it grows linearly. Total amount A = P + I = P(1 + RT/100). Useful for short-term loans and basic calculations.

Compound interest: interest is calculated on the TOTAL accumulated amount (principal + previous interest). Formula: A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ where n is the number of compounding periods. Grows exponentially.
Comparing investments: for the same principal and rate, compound interest always gives more than simple interest after the first period. The longer the time, the greater the difference.
Depreciation (losing value): A = P(1 - r/100)ⁿ. Same structure as compound interest but the multiplier is less than 1. Examples: cars, equipment, technology depreciating in value.
Best buy: divide price by quantity to find unit cost. Lower unit cost = better value. Example: 500g for £1.20 → 0.24p/g vs 750g for £1.65 → 0.22p/g → 750g is better value.
Percentage problems: VAT (Value Added Tax) in UK = 20%. Price including VAT = original × 1.20. Original price (excl. VAT) = price incl. VAT ÷ 1.20.
Wages: gross pay = salary before deductions. Net pay = take-home after tax and NI. Basic pay + overtime. Overtime rate (time-and-a-half = × 1.5). Annual to weekly: ÷ 52. Annual to monthly: ÷ 12.
Exchange rates: multiply or divide by the given rate. Careful about direction: to convert GBP to EUR, multiply by the rate (£1 = €1.17 → £200 = €234).
Loans and mortgages: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) — the true annual cost of borrowing including all charges. Higher APR = more expensive loan.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
flashcards.a: Simple interest: calculated only on the original principal. I = PRT/100. Grows linearly. Compound interest: calculated on the current total (principal + accumulated interest). A = P(1+r/100)ⁿ. Grows exponentially. Example: £1000 at 5% for 3 years. Simple: I=150, total=£1150. Compound: 1000×1.05³=£1157.63. Compound is always more after the first period.

flashcards.q: A car costs £15,000 and depreciates at 12% per year. Find its value after 4 years.
Find the original price if a jacket costs £85.80 after a 35% discount.
flashcards.a: Price after 35% off = original × 0.65. So original = 85.80 ÷ 0.65 = £132. Check: 132 × 0.65 = £85.80 ✓. Common error: adding 35% to £85.80 = £115.83 (WRONG — this finds 35% of the discounted price, not the original).

flashcards.q: Which is better: 500g of coffee for £4.50 or 750g for £6.45?
flashcards.a: 500g: £4.50 ÷ 500 = 0.9p per gram. 750g: £6.45 ÷ 750 = 0.86p per gram. The 750g pack is better value (lower price per gram). Always find the price per unit (gram, litre, etc.) and compare.

flashcards.q: £2,500 is invested for 3 years at 4% per annum compound interest. Find the total interest earned.
flashcards.a: A = 2500 × (1.04)³ = 2500 × 1.124864 = £2,812.16. Interest earned = £2,812.16 - £2,500 = £312.16. For simple interest at same rate: I = 2500×4×3/100 = £300. Compound interest earns £12.16 more over 3 years.

flashcards.q: What is frequency density?
flashcards.a: Frequency ÷ class width — always the y-axis on a histogram

flashcards.q: How do you find the frequency from a histogram bar?
flashcards.a: Frequency = frequency density × class width (area of the bar)

flashcards.q: What is a stratified sample?
flashcards.a: A sample where each group is represented proportionally: (group size ÷ population) × sample size

flashcards.q: What is systematic sampling?
flashcards.a: Select every nth item from a list after a random start — e.g. every 10th person on a register

flashcards.q: What is a biased sample?
flashcards.a: A sample that does not accurately represent the population — certain groups are over- or under-represented

flashcards.q: What is a scatter graph used for?
flashcards.a: Showing the relationship (correlation) between two variables

flashcards.q: What is positive correlation?
flashcards.a: As one variable increases, the other increases — points slope upward from left to right

flashcards.q: What does no correlation look like?
flashcards.a: Points scattered randomly with no pattern — the variables are not related

flashcards.q: What is a line of best fit?
flashcards.a: A straight line drawn through the middle of the points on a scatter graph — equal numbers of points above and below

flashcards.q: What is interpolation vs extrapolation?
flashcards.a: Interpolation: estimating within the data range (more reliable). Extrapolation: estimating outside the data range (less reliable)

tips.t: AQA higher tier: if asked to compare simple and compound interest, always calculate both and compare. Simple interest grows linearly; compound grows exponentially. For short periods and low rates, the difference is small. Compound always wins over very long periods.

The most common financial maths error: to find the ORIGINAL price before a % change, always DIVIDE by the multiplier (not add/subtract a percentage of the new value). Price after 20% VAT = £120. Original = 120÷1.20=£100. NEVER 120-20%=120-24=£96 (that is 20% of the new price, not the original).

quiz.q: A laptop costs £840 including 20% VAT. What is the pre-VAT price?
quiz.exp: Price including VAT = original × 1.20. Original = 840 ÷ 1.20 = £700. Common mistake: 840 - 20% = 840 - 168 = £672. WRONG — 20% of £840 ≠ 20% of the original price. Always divide by the multiplier to reverse a percentage change.

quiz.exp: Year 0: £12,000. Year 1: 12000×0.82=£9,840. Year 2: 9840×0.82=£8,069. Year 3: 8069×0.82=£6,617 (<£7,000). After 3 years, the car is worth approximately £6,617, which is less than £7,000.

quiz.q: Simple interest on £2,000 at 6% per annum for 3 years is:
quiz.exp: I = PRT/100 = 2000×6×3/100 = £360. Total amount = £2,360. For compound interest: 2000×(1.06)³=£2,382.03. Simple interest is just I=360, not the total amount.

quiz.exp: Taxable income = 28,000 - 12,570 = £15,430. Tax = 20% of £15,430 = 0.20 × 15,430 = £3,086. Income tax is only charged on earnings ABOVE the personal allowance threshold.

quiz.q: £1 = €1.15. How many pounds do you get for €460?

opts: Q = P + PRT/100
Q = P × r × n
quiz.exp: Compound interest formula: A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. P=principal (initial), r=rate per period (%), n=number of periods. The multiplier (1+r/100) is applied n times. For depreciation, use (1-r/100)ⁿ. Simple interest: A=P(1+RT/100) (linear, not exponential).

opts: Compound is always better for long periods
theta over 360 times pi r squared where theta is the angle in degrees

quiz.exp: A=2400×(1.08)²=2400×1.1664=£2,799.36. Wait: 1.08²=1.1664. 2400×1.1664=2799.36. Let me check the options: £2,795.52 ≠ 2799.36. Perhaps: 2400×1.08=2592, 2592×1.08=2799.36. quiz.q: Histograms differ from bar charts because:
opts: The area of each bar (not the height) represents the frequency — used for grouped continuous data with unequal class widths

quiz.exp: Histogram: frequency density = frequency / class width. Area of bar = frequency. Equal class widths: heights AND areas proportional to frequency. Unequal class widths: heights NOT proportional to frequency — must use frequency density. The y-axis: labelled 'frequency density', not 'frequency'. Common error: drawing histogram with frequency on y-axis when class widths are unequal — this misrepresents the data.

facts: Pi (π) has been calculated to over 100 trillion decimal places — it is irrational, meaning the digits never repeat or terminate.
The equals sign (=) was invented by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557 — he chose two parallel lines because 'no two things can be more equal'.
Every even integer greater than 2 appears to be expressible as the sum of two primes (Goldbach's Conjecture, 1742) — but this has never been proved.

proQuiz.q: What does "perceptive" mean in AQA mark scheme language for Mathematics?
opts: Simply correct and detailed
Showing insight beyond the obvious — making non-trivial connections, noticing subtle implications, offering original interpretations that demonstrate deep understanding
Writing at length
Using complex vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Perceptive is AQA's highest-level analytical descriptor. It implies going beyond the explicitly stated to infer, interpret, and connect ideas in original ways. Perceptive students notice what is NOT said as much as what IS said.

proQuiz.q: You understand Financial Mathematics deeply if you can:
opts: Recite your notes from memory
Apply the concepts to unfamiliar exam questions, explain them in your own words, identify connections to other topics, and evaluate conflicting evidence confidently
Re-read your notes without hesitation
Score 100% on a familiar quiz
proQuiz.exp: True mastery = transfer. If you can only answer questions you've seen before, you have surface learning. Deep learning enables flexible application to ANY question on the topic, regardless of phrasing or context.

proQuiz.q: For Financial Mathematics, which study approach creates the deepest understanding?
opts: Re-reading textbook chapters
Trying to TEACH the concept to someone else (real or imaginary) — the effort of explanation forces you to identify gaps and restructure knowledge
Making colourful notes
Listening to recorded lessons
proQuiz.exp: The protege effect: teaching consolidates understanding. When you explain a concept, you identify precisely where your understanding breaks down — this guides targeted revision. The Feynman technique: if you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it deeply.

proQuiz.q: When writing a conclusion for an extended Mathematics answer:
opts: Simply repeat your first point
Directly answer the question stating which argument is most significant and why
Write a new argument not in the body
Write: in conclusion there are many factors
proQuiz.exp: Effective conclusions: directly answer the question using on balance or therefore. State your overall judgement with reasoning. Base it on body evidence only. Never introduce new points in a conclusion.

proTip: Pro Tip for Mathematics - Financial Mathematics: Always use specific evidence, precise terminology, and evaluate every claim. Structure: point + evidence + analysis + evaluation. Target your weakest sub-topics using your quiz results.

name: Problem Solving & Proof

points: Reading the question: underline key information, identify what you are asked to FIND (not just calculate), check the units required, check if an exact answer or decimal is needed.
Form an equation: translate worded problems into algebra. Introduce a variable, write expressions for the quantities, form and solve an equation.
Systematic listing: list all possibilities in order. Use sample space diagrams, tree diagrams, or tables. Useful for counting problems and probability.
Reverse working: when given the result, work backwards applying inverse operations step by step.
Algebraic proof: use letters to represent general numbers — never use specific values. Show both sides of an equation are equal, or that an expression always has a required property.

Proof that a number is always even/odd: an even number = 2n. An odd number = 2n+1. Sum of two evens: 2n+2m=2(n+m) = even. Sum of even and odd: 2n+(2m+1)=2(n+m)+1 = odd. Product of two odds: (2n+1)(2m+1)=4nm+2n+2m+1=2(2nm+n+m)+1 = odd.
Counter-example: to DISPROVE a conjecture, find one example where it fails. Example: "all prime numbers are odd" — disproved by p=2.
Proof by exhaustion: prove a statement for all cases by checking each one. Only practical for finite small sets.
Geometric proof: use circle theorems, congruence conditions (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), angle rules with full reasoning and stated theorems.

flashcards.q: Prove that the product of two consecutive even numbers is divisible by 8.
flashcards.a: Let the two consecutive even numbers be 2n and 2n+2. Product = 2n(2n+2) = 2n × 2(n+1) = 4n(n+1). Now n and n+1 are consecutive integers, so one of them must be even. Therefore n(n+1) is divisible by 2. So 4n(n+1) is divisible by 4×2 = 8. ✓

flashcards.q: Prove that the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3.
flashcards.a: Let the integers be n, n+1, n+2. Sum = n+(n+1)+(n+2) = 3n+3 = 3(n+1). Since the sum equals 3 multiplied by an integer (n+1), it is always divisible by 3. ✓ AQA: use consecutive integers starting at n (not 1,2,3) to prove for ALL cases.

flashcards.q: Show by counter-example that the statement "n²+n+11 is prime for all positive integers n" is false.
flashcards.a: Try n=11: n²+n+11 = 121+11+11 = 143 = 11×13. Since 143 is not prime (it has factors 11 and 13), the statement is false. A single counter-example is sufficient to disprove "for all" statements.

flashcards.q: A problem states: "The sum of two numbers is 15 and their difference is 3. Find the numbers." Form a system of equations.
flashcards.a: Let the two numbers be x and y (with x>y). Sum: x+y=15. Difference: x-y=3. Adding the equations: 2x=18, x=9. Then y=15-9=6. Check: 9+6=15 ✓ and 9-6=3 ✓. When forming equations from word problems, always define your variables clearly.

flashcards.q: Prove that (n+1)² - (n-1)² is always divisible by 4.
flashcards.a: Expand: (n+1)² = n²+2n+1. (n-1)² = n²-2n+1. Difference = (n²+2n+1)-(n²-2n+1) = 4n. Since 4n = 4×n, the result is always divisible by 4, for any integer n. ✓ This type of proof involves expanding and simplifying, then factorising to show divisibility.

flashcards.q: What is a derivative?
flashcards.a: The gradient function of a curve — tells you the rate of change at any point. GCSE: found by drawing a tangent

flashcards.q: What is a rate of change in context?
flashcards.a: How quickly one quantity changes relative to another — gradient of a graph in a real context

flashcards.q: How do you estimate the gradient of a curve?
flashcards.a: Draw a tangent (straight line touching curve at exactly one point) and calculate its gradient

flashcards.q: What does d/dx notation mean?
flashcards.a: The derivative of a function — 'differentiate with respect to x' (Higher GCSE / A-level)

flashcards.q: What is an area under a graph in a real context?
flashcards.a: Depends on the axes: velocity-time → distance; acceleration-time → velocity change

flashcards.q: How do you estimate the area under a curve?
flashcards.a: Divide into trapezoids or rectangles and sum their areas (trapezoid rule)

flashcards.q: What is a turning point on a graph?
flashcards.a: A maximum or minimum — the gradient is zero at this point (tangent is horizontal)

flashcards.q: What is a function notation like f(x)?
flashcards.a: f(x) means the output when x is the input. f(3) means substitute x=3

flashcards.q: What is a composite function fg(x)?
flashcards.a: Apply g first, then apply f to the result: fg(x) = f(g(x))

flashcards.q: What is an inverse function f⁻¹(x)?
flashcards.a: The function that undoes f — if f(x)=2x+1 then f⁻¹(x)=(x-1)/2

tips.t: AQA algebraic proof: (1) Define variables clearly (e.g. "let n be any integer"). (2) Show the algebra step by step. (3) Factorise to reveal the property. (4) Write a clear conclusion ("Therefore the expression is always even because it is a multiple of 2"). Never use numbers as examples in a proof — they only demonstrate, not prove.

To DISPROVE: you need just ONE counter-example. To PROVE "for all integers": you must use algebra. Check special cases first (n=0, n=1, n=-1, n=2) for counter-examples. For claims involving primes, always test n=2 (the only even prime — catches many false claims).

quiz.q: Prove or disprove: "The square of an odd number is always odd."
opts: Disproved because 1²=1 is odd but 3²=9 is not divisible by 3
Disproved by n=3: 9 is even
Largest value minus smallest value - a measure of spread
Proved: (2n+1)²=4n²+4n+1=2(2n²+2n)+1 which is odd
quiz.exp: (2n+1)² = 4n²+4n+1 = 2(2n²+2n)+1. This is in the form 2k+1 (where k=2n²+2n) which is odd. The square of any odd number is always odd. AQA: show the algebraic manipulation clearly and conclude with "which is odd because it is in the form 2k+1."

quiz.q: A number is doubled, then 5 is added. The result is 23. What is the original number?
quiz.exp: Let the number be x. 2x+5=23 → 2x=18 → x=9. Check: 2(9)+5=23 ✓. This is a simple "form an equation" strategy — define the variable, translate the words into algebra, solve.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a valid counter-example to "all square numbers are even"?
opts: 4 (even square)
9 (odd square)
16 (even square)
100 (even square)
quiz.exp: 9 = 3² is a square number that is ODD. This single counter-example disproves the conjecture. You only need ONE counter-example to disprove a universal statement. The statement is clearly false: 1,9,25,49... are all odd square numbers.

quiz.q: Prove that the difference between the squares of two consecutive odd numbers is divisible by 8.
opts: Frequency density on the y-axis - area of each bar represents frequency
Let them be 2n+1 and 2n+3. Difference = (2n+3)²-(2n+1)² = 8n+8 = 8(n+1), divisible by 8.
Let them be n and n+2. Difference = 4n+4 = 4(n+1), divisible by 4.
Let them be 2n-1 and 2n+1. Difference = 8n, divisible by 8.
quiz.exp: (2n+3)²-(2n+1)² = (4n²+12n+9)-(4n²+4n+1) = 8n+8 = 8(n+1). Since 8(n+1) is 8 times an integer, it is always divisible by 8. Both options B and D are valid proofs (using different starting representations of consecutive odd numbers).

quiz.q: The sum of angles in a polygon with n sides is S°. A regular octagon has how many degrees in each interior angle?
quiz.exp: Sum of interior angles = (n-2)×180 = (8-2)×180 = 6×180 = 1080°. Each interior angle of a regular octagon = 1080°÷8 = 135°. Exterior angle = 360°÷8 = 45°. Check: 135°+45°=180° ✓

quiz.q: Tom thinks: "Adding any two prime numbers always gives an even number." Is this true?
opts: Yes: primes are odd, two odds sum to even
No: 2+3=5 which is odd (counter-example)
Yes: all primes are odd so the sum is always even
No: some primes are even so the sum varies
quiz.exp: 2+3=5 is a counter-example. Tom's reasoning fails because 2 is PRIME and EVEN. If either prime is 2, odd+even=odd. The statement is only true if both primes are odd (i.e. both greater than 2). AQA: always check whether 2 is involved when making claims about prime numbers.

quiz.q: n is a positive integer. Show that 6n² + 12n + 6 is always divisible by 6.
opts: 6n²+12n+6 = 6(n²+2n+1) = 6(n+1)², which is 6 times a perfect square, always divisible by 6
Frequency density equals frequency divided by class width — area of bar equals frequency
sin inverse, cos inverse and tan inverse find the angle when given the ratio
Solving quadratics and finding the minimum or maximum of a quadratic
quiz.exp: 6n²+12n+6 = 6(n²+2n+1) = 6(n+1)². Since (n+1)² is a perfect square (always a non-negative integer), 6(n+1)² is always a multiple of 6, hence divisible by 6. The factorisation also shows it is divisible by 6.

quiz.q: A rectangle has perimeter 36 cm and area 80 cm². Form equations and find the dimensions.
quiz.exp: Perimeter: 2(l+w)=36 → l+w=18. Area: lw=80. From first: l=18-w. Substitute: (18-w)w=80 → 18w-w²=80 → w²-18w+80=0 → (w-8)(w-10)=0 → w=8 or w=10. Both give dimensions 10 cm × 8 cm (same rectangle).

quiz.q: Prove that (2n+3)² - (2n-1)² simplifies to a multiple of 16.
opts: It simplifies to 16n+8=8(2n+1), multiple of 8 not 16 unless n is odd
New minus Original divided by Original times 100
It simplifies to 8n+8=8(n+1), multiple of 8 not 16
quiz.exp: (2n+3)²-(2n-1)² = (4n²+12n+9)-(4n²-4n+1) = 16n+8 = 8(2n+1). This is always a multiple of 8 (since 8(2n+1) = 8×odd). It is NOT always a multiple of 16 — e.g. n=1: 16+8=24, and 24÷16 is not an integer.

quiz.q: The nth term of a sequence is n²-n+41. For which value of n does the formula first fail to give a prime?
quiz.exp: n=41: 41²-41+41=41²=1681=41×41. Since 1681 = 41², it is not prime. This famous example (Euler's prime-generating polynomial) gives primes for n=1 to 40, but fails at n=41. AQA: this type of question tests whether you can find the counter-example by systematic substitution.

quiz.q: Prove that the sum of a two-digit number and the number formed by reversing its digits is always divisible by 11.
opts: P of A given B equals P of A and B divided by P of B
True: 10a+b+10b+a=11a+11b=11(a+b), always divisible by 11
Need to know the specific digits
True: both numbers have same digit sum
quiz.exp: Let the two-digit number have tens digit a and units digit b. The number = 10a+b. Reversed = 10b+a. Sum = 10a+b+10b+a = 11a+11b = 11(a+b). Since 11(a+b) is 11 times an integer, the sum is always divisible by 11. ✓

x equals negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4ac all divided by 2a

quiz.exp: Area under v-t graph = distance travelled. Rectangle: constant velocity. Triangle: uniform acceleration from/to rest. Trapezoid: uniform acceleration between two different velocities. For non-uniform acceleration (curved graph): estimate area by counting squares. The unit: multiply velocity unit (m/s) × time unit (s) = metres. Negative area (below x-axis): movement in the opposite direction.

facts: Pi (π) has been calculated to over 100 trillion decimal places — it is irrational, meaning the digits never repeat or terminate.
The equals sign (=) was invented by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557 — he chose two parallel lines because 'no two things can be more equal'.
Every even integer greater than 2 appears to be expressible as the sum of two primes (Goldbach's Conjecture, 1742) — but this has never been proved.

definitions.def: Expressing a number as a product of its prime factors — the unique building blocks of every positive integer.
A number that cannot be expressed as a fraction p/q where p and q are integers — e.g. π, √2, e.
The meaningful digits in a number, starting from the first non-zero digit.

proQuiz.q: Which command word in English Language requires the most complex response?
opts: State
Describe
Evaluate — requires weighing evidence and reaching a justified conclusion
List
proQuiz.exp: Evaluate is always the highest-order command word. It requires you to weigh evidence, consider perspectives, and make a justified judgement — not just describe or explain.

proQuiz.q: For a 6-mark extended answer on Problem Solving & Proof, which is essential?
opts: As many facts as possible
Specific terminology + clear argument + evidence + evaluation
Only diagrams
One-word answers
proQuiz.exp: 6-mark answers require quality reasoning using precise terminology, with specific evidence linked to a clear evaluative argument. Quantity without quality scores Level 1.

proQuiz.q: A student scores 45% on a Problem Solving & Proof quiz. The best next step is:
opts: Retake immediately
Move on
Review each wrong answer, identify the specific gap, revisit notes, then retest after 24 hours
Give up on this topic
proQuiz.exp: Targeted review: identify WHAT you misunderstand, not just THAT you got it wrong. Return to notes for those specific sub-topics. Retest after a gap for spaced repetition effect.

proQuiz.q: When asked to assess something in English Language, you should:
opts: List all relevant facts
Define key terms only
Weigh importance using specific evidence then reach a justified conclusion
Describe the process
proQuiz.exp: Assess = weigh and judge. Consider multiple factors, provide evidence, decide which factor is most significant and explain why. Every point must be evaluated, not just described.

proQuiz.q: Which distinguishes a Grade 9 from a Grade 7 response in English Language?
opts: Length
Quantity of facts
Consistent perceptive evaluative analysis — non-obvious insights, significance evaluation, nuanced conclusions
Handwriting quality
proQuiz.exp: AQA Grade 9: perceptive, convincing, nuanced. Grade 7: detailed, clear, well-developed. Grade 9 requires going beyond description to genuine insight and evaluation throughout the response.

proQuiz.q: For 9-mark questions in English Language, the most effective structure is:
opts: Three points as a list
Introduction + 3 developed analytical points with evidence + counterargument + conclusion with overall judgement
Just one very long point
Only counterarguments
proQuiz.exp: 9-mark structure: three analytical points (each with claim + evidence + analysis) + counterargument + conclusion that directly answers the question with a justified verdict.

proQuiz.q: How should you use specific data in English Language exam answers?
opts: Avoid numbers as they might be wrong
Include specific figures, dates, and named examples to support each claim — vague answers score much lower
Only in science subjects
At the end of answers only
proQuiz.exp: Specific evidence: named examples, precise statistics, exact dates score more than vague claims. The specificity demonstrates genuine knowledge rather than generic understanding.

proQuiz.q: Interleaving Problem Solving & Proof with other topics during revision is beneficial because:
opts: It is easier
It creates retrieval challenges that build stronger, more flexible memory traces
It covers topics superficially
It reduces study time significantly
proQuiz.exp: Interleaving (mixing topics in one session) is more effortful but produces better retention than blocked study. The brain is forced to identify which knowledge applies — building flexible, transferable understanding.

proQuiz.q: A model answer for Problem Solving & Proof should be used to:
opts: Memorise word for word
Analyse why it scores highly — structure, evidence, connectives, terminology — then practise the same SKILLS independently
Submit as your own work
Ignore since it was written by someone else
proQuiz.exp: Model answers reveal examiner expectations. Analyse: what structure did they use? Which evidence? What connectives? How is the conclusion phrased? Understand WHY it scores, then develop those skills yourself.

proQuiz.q: When revising Problem Solving & Proof, spaced retrieval practice means:
opts: Studying for long sessions without breaks
Testing yourself at increasing time intervals — day 1, day 3, day 7, day 14 — each session reinforcing memory traces
Reading notes repeatedly
Studying only the night before
proQuiz.exp: Spaced retrieval (Ebbinghaus): memory strength decays but is rebuilt stronger each time you retrieve it. Increasing the gaps between retrieval sessions maximises long-term retention with less total study time.

proQuiz.q: What makes evidence in English Language answers most persuasive?
opts: Using long quotations or data tables
Selecting the most directly relevant specific evidence, embedding it within your argument, and explaining precisely how it supports your claim
Including as much evidence as possible
Evidence from personal experience
proQuiz.exp: Evidence quality > quantity. One precisely relevant, well-interpreted piece of evidence scores higher than three loosely relevant ones. Always explain the connection: "This evidence suggests that... because..."

proQuiz.q: In extended writing about Problem Solving & Proof, which connectives best demonstrate analytical thinking?
opts: And, but, also
Therefore, consequently, this demonstrates that, nevertheless, on balance, this suggests — creating logical chains between evidence and argument
However is the only useful connective
Connectives are not important
proQuiz.exp: Analytical connectives create explicit logical chains: evidence + therefore + interpretation + however + counterargument + on balance + conclusion. They show the examiner HOW your evidence supports your argument.

proQuiz.q: Why is it important to address counterarguments in extended answers?
opts: It is not — just argue one side strongly
Acknowledging and refuting counterarguments shows sophisticated understanding and strengthens your position by demonstrating you have considered the full picture
Present only counterarguments
The counterargument should be your conclusion
proQuiz.exp: Counterarguments demonstrate: understanding of complexity, that your position has survived scrutiny, and analytical sophistication. Some argue X, however this is outweighed by Y because Z — this structure scores Level 4.

proQuiz.q: What is the difference between an assertion and an argument in English Language?
opts: They are identical
An assertion states a claim without support. An argument provides claim + evidence + reasoning linking the two. Assertions score Level 1-2; arguments score Level 3-4.
Arguments are longer than assertions
Assertions use better vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Assertion: X is important. Argument: X is the most significant factor because Y (evidence), which demonstrates Z, making it more influential than alternative A due to B. The mechanism and comparative judgement elevate assertion to argument.

proQuiz.q: Past exam papers for Problem Solving & Proof are best used by:
opts: Reading them without attempting
Attempting under timed conditions, then self-marking rigorously, identifying your current level, studying Level 4 exemplars, and practising specific identified weaknesses
Only reading the mark scheme
Skipping difficult questions
proQuiz.exp: Past paper practice cycle: (1) attempt under exam conditions; (2) mark against official mark scheme; (3) identify level achieved; (4) study Level 4 responses to see what Level 4 requires; (5) practise the specific skills you lack.

proQuiz.q: How does the testing effect help with Problem Solving & Proof?
opts: Testing is discouraging and should be avoided
Being tested on material — even before feeling ready — improves long-term retention more than equivalent re-study time. Retrieval strengthens memory traces.
Testing only measures not improves learning
Testing works only for factual recall
proQuiz.exp: Testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006): retrieval practice is one of the most effective learning strategies. The effort of trying to recall information strengthens the memory trace even more than re-reading. Struggle during recall is a sign of productive learning.

proQuiz.q: What does "perceptive" mean in AQA mark scheme language for English Language?
opts: Simply correct and detailed
Showing insight beyond the obvious — making non-trivial connections, noticing subtle implications, offering original interpretations that demonstrate deep understanding
Writing at length
Using complex vocabulary
proQuiz.exp: Perceptive is AQA's highest-level analytical descriptor. It implies going beyond the explicitly stated to infer, interpret, and connect ideas in original ways. Perceptive students notice what is NOT said as much as what IS said.

proQuiz.q: You understand Problem Solving & Proof deeply if you can:
opts: Recite your notes from memory
Apply the concepts to unfamiliar exam questions, explain them in your own words, identify connections to other topics, and evaluate conflicting evidence confidently
Re-read your notes without hesitation
Score 100% on a familiar quiz
proQuiz.exp: True mastery = transfer. If you can only answer questions you've seen before, you have surface learning. Deep learning enables flexible application to ANY question on the topic, regardless of phrasing or context.

proQuiz.q: For Problem Solving & Proof, which study approach creates the deepest understanding?
opts: Re-reading textbook chapters
Trying to TEACH the concept to someone else (real or imaginary) — the effort of explanation forces you to identify gaps and restructure knowledge
Making colourful notes
Listening to recorded lessons
proQuiz.exp: The protege effect: teaching consolidates understanding. When you explain a concept, you identify precisely where your understanding breaks down — this guides targeted revision. The Feynman technique: if you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it deeply.

proQuiz.q: When writing a conclusion for an extended English Language answer:
opts: Simply repeat your first point
Directly answer the question stating which argument is most significant and why
Write a new argument not in the body
Write: in conclusion there are many factors
proQuiz.exp: Effective conclusions: directly answer the question using on balance or therefore. State your overall judgement with reasoning. Base it on body evidence only. Never introduce new points in a conclusion.

proTip: Pro Tip for English Language - Problem Solving & Proof: Always use specific evidence, precise terminology, and evaluate every claim. Structure: point + evidence + analysis + evaluation. Target your weakest sub-topics using your quiz results.
